annotations.text: We combine repeated evaluations, controlled task variations, and lifecycle interventions to examine whether improvements from skill evolution persist and transfer, and to trace their origins to feedback, revision, selection, skill content, and evaluation.

annotations.text: We organize the evidence as a diagnosis of utility, behavioral scope, and gain attribution. Standard-task evaluations of SkillEvolver, SPARK, and CoEvoSkills first establish the observed utility of completed artifacts across two runs. Controlled task changes then reveal different scopes of usefulness, and artifact and trace inspection examines the decisions preserved during reuse. This motivates the next diagnostic step: locating an improvement in the artifact's evolution history. Complementary studies of SkillRevise, SkillHone, and SkillOpt use retention tests and lifecycle interventions to examine trace-conditioned revision, history-based iterative honing, and validation-gated editing. Each study addresses a specific part of the identification question.

annotations.text: 3. DIAGNOSING THE SCOPE OF SKILL UTILITY
annotations.comment: 新增实验：标准任务与变体结果、技能复用实例，以及基于两篇方法论文的反馈机制解释。

annotations.text: The first diagnostic question is where a completed skill is useful. A positive source-task result can arise from content that applies across instances or from a procedure fitted to the original task. We dis- tinguish these possibilities by first examining paired utility in two standard-task runs, then deploying frozen skills under three forms of task variation. Inspection of skill content and execution traces con- nects the resulting utility profiles to decisions made during deploy- ment.

annotations.text: 3.2. Source-Task Gains Recur across Runs

annotations.text: All three methods have positive mean paired gains in both runs (Ta- ble 1). SkillEvolver gains 25.61 and 25.02 points, CoEvoSkills gains 10.24 and 9.76, and SPARK gains 1.84 and 6.45. SkillEvolver and CoEvoSkills retain similar gains despite substantial changes in their no-skill scores. Their benefit is therefore more consistent across runs than their absolute skill-condition scores suggest. The task-level results also differ. SkillEvolver has at least four times as many improvements as regressions in each run; CoEvoSkills improves 17 tasks in each run, with nine and ten regressions. SPARK’s first run is nearly balanced, while its second has 13 im- provements and five regressions. These results establish recurring source-task utility. We next ask whether the same frozen skills re- main useful after the task changes.

annotations.text: The complete record contains 222 variants and 886 condition- level results across no skill and the three methods. Table 2 summa- rizes historical and recovery evaluations for 222 SkillEvolver vari- ants and 221 each for SPARK and CoEvoSkills, pairing each skill condition with the no-skill result on the same variant. Source-task improvement does not imply useful generalization. All three methods improve mean reward on the source tasks in both runs, but their variant results diverge. SkillEvolver retains a positive mean gain of 11.94 points, SPARK is close to neutral at +0.65, and CoEvoSkills falls below the no-skill baseline at −5.01. SkillEvolver also improves more variants than it regresses (47 versus 20), whereas SPARK and CoEvoSkills show the reverse. Thus, the source-task

annotations.text: gains of the latter two methods do not translate into a consistent ad- vantage on changed tasks. Replacing the instance produces the largest divergence. SkillE- volver remains positive under all three changes, with its largest gain on P2 (+14.56). P2 is also where SPARK and CoEvoSkills de- cline most (−5.23 and −9.51). SPARK retains positive averages un- der representation and requirement changes, but loses its advantage when the underlying instance changes. SkillEvolver’s positive re- sults across P1–P3 indicate a broader observed scope of skill utility. CoEvoSkills’ negative averages across all three changes show that its source-task benefit is particularly sensitive to reuse conditions.

annotations.text: Successful skills retain guidance for choosing and checking. In exoplanet detection, the SkillEvolver skill supports successful de- tection after input columns are rearranged (P1) and after the task requires two signals (P3). The CoEvoSkills skill fails both variants: its use leads to stellar modulation being reported as the target sig- nal, and a signal and its harmonic being treated as two separate sig- nals. The SkillEvolver skill explicitly organizes candidate discovery, signal diagnosis, and refinement, including checks for misleading peaks. This case suggests that preserving criteria for accepting a re- sult can be more useful under task changes than retaining a search routine alone. Both skills fail the replacement-instance P2 variant, so the successful checks address only part of this task family’s vari- ation. A similar distinction appears in scheduling. The SkillEvolver and SPARK skills succeed on all three variants; the CoEvoSkills skill succeeds only on P3. In P1, using the CoEvoSkills skill yields an otherwise valid schedule that fails the requirement to place each operation at its earliest feasible time. The SkillEvolver skill explic- itly includes this local-minimality requirement and baseline-relative repair rules. Here, successful reuse depends on preserving the task’s repair conditions in the skill. The feedback used to build a skill helps explain its contents. The two methods differ in how they turn experience into revisions. SkillEvolver compares successful and failed deployments of a candi- date skill, then patches guidance that was missing or misleading. Its independent audit also checks for reliance on training-instance con- stants [5]. These mechanisms directly target both omitted conditions and instance-specific assumptions. The rules retained in our schedul- ing and signal-detection skills are consistent with that emphasis: they describe what to check when reusing a procedure. CoEvoSkills obtains detailed revision feedback from a co-

annotations.text: evolving surrogate verifier; the ground-truth oracle returns only an opaque pass/fail signal [7]. Consequently, discovering an omitted condition depends on the surrogate reconstructing it from the task and observed outputs. This offers a plausible explanation for a skill that covers many feasibility checks but misses a condition needed for successful reuse, as in the scheduling example. Both methods gen- erate reusable skill packages; the relevant difference is which failure information becomes persistent guidance. Our interpretation is that feedback coverage and abstraction from the source instance help de- termine the scope of the resulting skill. Connecting utility to the evolution process. The results identify useful skills and differences in their applicability; the examples sug- gest how retained guidance relates to those differences. The next studies test where improvements enter the lifecycle, using parent- to-final comparisons and interventions on feedback, selection, skill content, and verification in SkillRevise, SkillHone, and SkillOpt.

annotations.text: We diagnose where the gains from self-evolving persistent skills reside and how far they extend. All three methods in the standard-task evaluations have positive paired gains in both runs, but task variation separates their utility profiles. SkillEvolver remains positive across representation, instance, and requirement changes; SPARK combines gains on two probes with a decline on instance changes; CoEvoSkills declines on all three. The inspected traces identify decision criteria and correctness checks expressed during successful reuse. Complementary lifecycle interventions show that adopted artifact components can change behavior, selected outcomes can disappear under fresh deployment, and fixed outputs can receive different verdicts under different verifiers. Together, these findings distinguish useful artifacts, their behavioral scope, and the processes that produce or measure their apparent improvement.
